intro: Paderewski recorded Chopin’s Nocturne in F♯ major, Op. 15 No. 2 (Larghetto), in New York in May 1917. His playing uses rolled chords and lets the hands sound at different moments.

sections.label: A · Melody in F♯ major, Larghetto
sections.mNote: Decorated right-hand melody above bass notes and chords.

sections.label: B · Doppio movimento, dotted theme
sections.mNote: Doppio movimento begins sotto voce over a C♯ bass.

sections.label: A′ · Opening melody returns, F♯ major
sections.mNote: The opening tempo and melody return after a pause.

cues.title: Opening melody and accompaniment
cues.text: Chopin’s melody moves through quick ornaments while the left hand plays bass notes and chords beneath it. Paderewski’s playing often separates the attacks of the two hands and spreads chords, so that the melody sounds before or after its accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Opening piano writing: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 1–16, https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86. Jonathan Woolf discusses hand dislocation and arpeggiated chords across Paderewski’s Victor recordings: https://www.musicweb-international.com/classrev/2017/May/Paderewski_American_7505.htm

cues.title: Victor recording, New York, 1917
cues.text: On 14 May 1917 Paderewski recorded this nocturne for Victor in New York, and the company issued the first take. He returned on 18 June to record Chopin’s G♭ major Butterfly Étude.
cues.evidence: APR 7505 session listing: Nocturne, matrix C 19781-1, 14 May 1917; Étude Op. 25 No. 9, 18 June 1917. https://www.musicweb-international.com/classrev/2017/May/Paderewski_American_7505.htm

cues.title: Central section, bars 25–40
cues.text: The central passage (bars 25–40) begins sotto voce, with a dotted tune set among quick accompanying notes. Chopin asks for twice the motion. The left hand leaps and the dotted patterns continue as the passage builds to the central climax.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 25–40; Mieczysław Tomaszewski discusses the dotted rhythms and central climax. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86; https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The repeated figures slow and descend. After a pause, A♯ rises to B, the turn that opens the nocturne. The theme returns with its original outline, and Chopin adds new ornaments to it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–52. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paderewski on rubato, 1909
cues.text: In his 1909 essay on rubato, Paderewski mocked the rule that time borrowed from one phrase must be repaid in another. “What is lost is lost,” he wrote. “For any lawlessness there is, after a certain term, proscription.”
cues.evidence: Ignacy Jan Paderewski, ‘Tempo Rubato’, in Henry T. Finck, Success in Music and How It Is Won (1909), chapter 28, pp. 454–461; reprinted by the USC Polish Music Center: https://polishmusic.usc.edu/research/publications/polish-music-journal/vol4no1/paderewski-tempo-rubato/

transitions.title: The bass turns to C♯
transitions.from: A · Melody in F♯ major, Larghetto
transitions.how: The slow section has repeated A♯s. A C♯ bass begins the middle section and supports a dominant seventh with E♯, G♯ and B. At Doppio movimento the motion doubles, and the right hand plays both a dotted tune and quick notes beneath it. The opening of the passage is marked sotto voce.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 24–26. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

transitions.title: Return of the opening tune
transitions.to: A′ · Opening melody returns, F♯ major
transitions.how: In bars 47–50 of the Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, Chopin writes molto rallentando, smorzando over repeated figures above a low C♯. The left hand then stops. After a pause, A♯ and B lead into the opening tune at its first tempo, and the bass moves from C♯ to F♯ beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, bars 47–50. https://chopinscores.org/partytura/86

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
